IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Vancouver,

[
1
]

This is an application by the plaintiff Ashraf Rezaei
Pour (“Ms. Pour”) under Rule 9-5 to strike out the pleadings in the counterclaim
of the defendants Amnis Engineering Ltd., Glen Ichikawa and Kawa Engineering
Ltd. (collectively, “the Amnis defendants”).

[
2
]

Ms. Pour seeks to strike out the
counterclaim of the Amnis defendants for defamation, abuse of process,
malicious prosecution and interference with contractual relations and interference
with economic relations.

[
3
]

Briefly, Ms. Pour is one of four

plaintiffs,
all members of the same family, who commenced an action against Mr. Ichikawa,
Amnis Engineering Ltd. (“Amnis”) and 10 other corporate defendants in 2015 for various
different claims including wrongful dismissal and moneys allegedly owed to them
for work they did as employees of Amnis. The plaintiffs have discontinued their
action against some of the corporate defendants.

[
4
]

Ms. Pour in particular claims compensation in
the amount of $43,642.86 for what she alleges are two years of unpaid food
services she says she provided Amnis employees at Mr. Ichikawa’s request.

[
5
]

On March 25, 2015, in response to the original
action in which Ms. Pour was one of four plaintiffs, the Amnis defendants
filed a counterclaim against all four plaintiffs. In their counterclaim the
Amnis defendants allege that all the plaintiffs, including Ms. Pour,
engaged in a concerted effort to cause them injury.

[
6
]

The counterclaim alleges that publications which
were sent by Amir Yashar Shoolestani with the concurrence of the other plaintiffs
were defamatory. Secondly, the Amnis defendants also allege that the legal
action commenced by the Shoolestani family, including Ms. Pour, amounted
to malicious prosecution and an abuse of process. In light of the Amnis
defendants’ submissions, the specific language used in the counterclaim is of
some significance in this application, as will be made clear shortly. The
relevant portions of the counterclaim read as follows:

DEFAMATION

8.         On
Thursday, March 19, 2009 at 6:04 a.m., in an email to Ryan Hanson of Innergex
Renewable Energy Inc. with copies to Jean Trudel and Innergex Renewable Energy
Inc., Amir Yashr Shoolestani wrote and published a number of statement
regarding Glen Ichikawa and Amnis Engineering Ltd., including but not limited
to:

(a)        Glen
Ichikawa has been paying only himself while charging the design work of his
engineers to the clients including Innergex;

(b)        Amnis
Engineering Ltd. does not have engineers competent to perform the work required
for the Innergex project; and

(c)        Glen
Ichikawa will falsely represent the receptionist as a draftsman.

9.         On March 29, 2009 at 5:52 p.m. in
an email to Paul Wearmouth and Dave Clarke of Peter Kiewit Sons Co., Amir Yashr
Shoolestani wrote and published a number of statements, including, but not
limited to:

(a)        Glen
Ichikawa is destroying evidence and your personal files;

(b)        Amnis
Engineering Ltd. has not correctly calculated the joint efficiency of the out
of spec welds; and

(c)        Glen
Ichikawa and Amnis Engineering Ltd. have been or will be covering up evidence.

10.       On or about March 19, 2009 and
March 29, 2009 Amir Yashr Shoolestani and Amir Behzad Shoolestani verbally made
the same statements described in paragraphs 8 and 9 of this Counterclaim on
separate occasions to Ryan Hanson of Innergex Renewable Energy Inc. and Dave Clarke
of Peter Kiewit Sons Co.

11.       The words were false and
defamatory of Glen Ichikawa and Amnis Engineering Ltd. in their natural and
ordinary meaning including any implied meanings.

12.       The words meant, were intended to
mean, and were understood to mean:

(a)        Glen
Ichikawa was illegally and immorally not paying his engineers;

(b)        Amnis
Engineering Ltd. did not have competent engineers;

(c)        Glen
Ichikawa was a liar and would destroy evidence and cover up evidence; and

(d)        Amnis
Engineering Ltd. has made a critical engineering error with respect to a design
it completed.

13.       The words were published
maliciously and were calculated to cause pecuniary damage to Glen Ichikawa and
Amnis Engineering Ltd. in respect of their business and employment.

14.       Although the emails were sent by
Amir Yashr Shoolestani, the emails were with the agreement and concurrence of
the other Defendants by Counterclaim and the other Defendants by Counterclaim
are equally responsible and liable for the emails.

15.       Although the works were spoken by
Amir Yashr Shoolestani and Amir Behzad Shoolestani, the words were spoken with
the agreement and concurrence of the other Defendants by Counterclaim and the
other Defendants by Counterclaim are equally responsible for the words spoken.

16.       As a result of the words, Glen
Ichikawa and Amnis Engineering Ltd. have suffered and continue to suffer,
damage to their business and reputation and the case of Glen Ichikawa damage to
his feelings.

17.       By letter dated March 31, 2009
Glen Ichikawa and Amnis Engineering Ltd., through their solicitor, provided a
detailed written complaint and requested a retraction and apology.

18.       The Defendants by Counterclaim did
not publish a retraction or apology.

19.       The statements made constitute a
defamation of the personal and professional reputation of Glen Ichikawa and
Amnis Engineering Ltd.

CLAIMS RELATING TO COMMENCEMENT OF THIS
ACTION

20.       On March 2, 2015 the Defendants by
Counterclaim (the “Plaintiffs”) commenced this action against the Plaintiffs by
Counterclaim and eleven other defendants that were, either directly or
indirectly, clients of Amnis Engineering Ltd. (the “Clients”).

21.       The Plaintiffs allege in their
Notice of Civil Claim that there employees of Amnis Engineering Ltd.

22.       The Plaintiffs allege in
paragraphs 14 to 19 of their Notice of Civil Claim that the clients were
clients of Amnis Engineering Ltd. and that Amnis Engineering Ltd. acted as a
consultant to the Clients.

23.       The Plaintiffs do not advance any
claim for relief against the Clients.

24.       The Plaintiffs do not describe any
basis upon which a legal claim could be advanced against the Clients.

25.       There is no basis in law for the
Plaintiffs to advance a claim against any of the Clients.

26.       The Plaintiffs, and each of them,
have conspired to injure Glen Ichikawa, Amnis Engineering Ltd., and Kawa
Engineering Ltd. by bringing this Notice of Civil Claim.

27.       The Plaintiffs have brought this
action against the Clients without reasonable and probable cause and
maliciously or with a purpose other than that of carrying the law into effect.
The Plaintiffs purpose was to create difficulty in the contractual and economic
relations between the Clients and the Plaintiffs by Counterclaim.

28.       The Plaintiffs’ conduct constitutes
malicious prosecution.

29.       Alternatively, the Plaintiffs’
conduct amounts to an abuse of process.

30.       Alternatively, the Plaintiffs’
conduct amount to an interference with contractual relations or an interference
with economic relations;

31.       The Plaintiffs by Counterclaim
have and will suffer injury, damage and loss as a result of the interference
with relations with the Clients.

32.       The Plaintiffs’ conduct
constitutes a wanton and outrageous disregard of the rights of the Plaintiffs
by Counterclaim for the Plaintiffs by Counterclaim are entitled to punitive,
exemplary and aggravated damages.

Part 2: RELIEF SOUGHT

1.         Damages
for defamation;

2.
Damages for malicious falsehood;

3.         Damages
for conspiracy;

4.         Damages
for malicious prosecution;

5.         Damages
for abuse of process;

6.         Damages
for interference with contractual relations and economic relations;

7.         Punitive,
exemplary and aggravated damages;

8.         Interest
pursuant to the
Court Order Interest Act
, RSBC 1996 c. 79;

9.         Costs.

[
7
]

In this application, the plaintiff Ms. Pour
seeks to have the counterclaim struck out in its entirety.

[
8
]

In support of her application, Ms. Pour
advances five main arguments as to why the counterclaim against her should be
struck. Firstly, Ms. Pour claims that the Amnis defendants (the plaintiffs
by counterclaim) were out of time when they filed their counterclaim. Secondly,
Ms. Pour argues that the counterclaim is not related to the subject matter
of her initiating claim. This second factor relates to the limitation argument
but also stands on its own to some extent. The third reason why the counterclaim
should be struck under Rule 9-5, according to Ms. Pour, is that the
pleadings do not reveal a cause of action against her, but only against Amir
Yashar Shoolestani and Amir Behzad Shoolestani. The fourth reason is that the
claim was not properly pleaded. This relates to the defamation claim and to
discrepancies between the email statements as they are cited in the counterclaim
and the original emails themselves. The fifth argument Ms. Pour raises in both
her oral and written submissions relates solely to the malicious prosecution
claim. She argues that a claim for malicious prosecution can only be made once
the proceeding which is the subject of that claim has come to an end. Since Ms. Pour’s
claim is still extant, the defendants cannot raise a claim for malicious
prosecution at this time.

[
9
]

Before turning the each of the specific
arguments raised by Ms. Pour, I set out the legal framework for an
application under Rule 9-5. Rule 9-5 reads as follows:

Rule 9-5 – Striking Pleadings

Scandalous, frivolous or vexatious
matters

(1) At any stage of a proceeding, the court
may order to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of a pleading,
petition or other document on the ground that

(a) it discloses
no reasonable claim or defence, as the case may be,

(b) it is
unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious,

(c) it may
prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial or hearing of the proceeding, or

(d) it is
otherwise an abuse of the process of the court,

and the court may pronounce judgment or
order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and may order the costs of the
application to be paid as special costs.

Admissibility of evidence

(2) No evidence
is admissible on an application under subrule (1) (a).

[
10
]

The grounds for striking pleadings pursuant to
Rule 9-5(1) were summarized by this Court in
Gateway Building Management
Limited v. Manjit Singh Randhawa
,
2013 BCSC 350
:

[16]      The test to be applied to
determine whether an action should be struck out as disclosing no reasonable
claim requires a conclusion that, assuming that the facts as stated or even if
amended are true, those facts disclose no cause of action, the pleadings
disclose no arguable issue, and it is plain and obvious that the claim cannot
succeed. If there is a chance that the action may succeed, then the Petition
and the Action should be allowed to proceed:
Hunt v. Cary Canada Inc.
,
1990
CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959.

[17]      In
Dempsey v. Envision Credit Union
,

2006 BCSC 750 (CanLII)
, Garson J., as she then was, provided the following
summary of Rule 9‑5 jurisprudence:

In summary, a
pleading will be struck out if:

(a)        the
pleadings are unintelligible, confusing and difficult to understand (
Citizens
for Foreign aid Reform
, [
Citizens of Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian
Jewish Congress
(1999),
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, 36 C.P.C. (4th) 266
(B.C.S.C.) ]);

(b)        the
pleadings do not establish a cause of action and do not advance a claim known
in law (
Citizens for Foreign aid Reform
,
supra
);

(c)        the
pleadings are without substance in that they are groundless, fanciful and
trifle with the Court’s time (
Borsato v. Basra
,
[2000 BCSC 28 (CanLII)
,
[2000] B.C.J. No. 84 (S.C.)])

(d)        the
pleadings are not bona fides, are oppressive and are designed to cause the
Defendants anxiety, trouble and expense (
Borsato v. Basra
,
supra
);

(e)        the
action is brought for an improper purpose, particularly the harassment and
oppression of the Defendants (
Ebrahim v. Ebrahim
,
2002 BCSC 466 (CanLII)
).

(at para. 17)

[18]      Pursuant
to Rule 9‑5, pleadings that are so prolix and confusing that it is
difficult, if not impossible, to understand the case to be met should also be
struck out:
The Owners, Strata Plan LMS3259 v. Sze Hang Holding Inc.
,
2009
BCSC 473 (CanLII)
, at para.
36
.

[
11
]

A procedural matter relating to the proper
interpretation of sub-Rule 9-5(2) was raised early on in this application.
Ms. Pour relies on affidavit evidence in support of her application.
Counsel for the Amnis defendants, on the other hand, submits that generally no
evidence should be admitted on an application under Rule 9-5. Instead the
facts alleged in the counterclaim are assumed to be true and a claim
will be struck only if it is plain and obvious that the pleading discloses
no reasonable cause of action on its face. In support of his argument Mr. Holeksa
relies on this Court’s ruling in
Rose v. British Columbia Life &
Casualty Company
,
2012 BCSC 1296
:

[3]        The recent and leading case of
R.
v. Imperial Tobacco Canada
,
2011 SCC 42 (CanLII)
, [2011] 3 S.C.R. 45,
confirmed the following propositions in relation to the former Rule 19(24)(a):

(i) A claim will
only be struck if it is plain and obvious, assuming the facts pleaded to be
true, that the pleading discloses no reasonable cause of action (at para. 17);

(ii) The power to
strike claims that have no reasonable prospect of success promotes efficiency
in the conduct of the litigation and contributes to more effective and fair
litigation (at para. 19); and

(iii) The motion to
strike is a tool that must be used with care, as the law is not static and
actions previously were deemed hopeless may in the future succeed. Therefore,
it is not determinative that the law has not yet recognized the particular
claim. In its analysis the court must be generous and err on the side of
permitting a novel but arguable claim to proceed to trial (at para. 21).

[4]        The
foregoing propositions are consistent with the conclusions and statements found
in cases such as
Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc
.,
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990]
2 S.C.R. 959 at 980,
Odhavi Estate v. Woodhouse
,
2003 SCC 69 (CanLII)
,
[2003] 3 S.C.R. 263 at para.
15
, and
Mohl v. University of British
Columbia
,
2006 BCCA 70 (CanLII)
at paras.
40 and 41
.

[
12
]

Ms. Pour, on the other hand relies on
Operation
Dismantle v. The Queen
,
1985 CanLII 74 (SCC)
, [1985] 1 SCR 441, where the Supreme Court of Canada
noted at para. 27 that:

We are not, in
my opinion, required by the principle enunciated in
Inuit Tapirisat
,
supra
,
to take as true the appellants’ allegations concerning the possible
consequences of the testing of the cruise missile. The rule that the material
facts in a statement of claim must be taken as true for the purpose of
determining whether it discloses a reasonable cause of action does not require
that allegations based on assumptions and speculations be taken as true. The
very nature of such an allegation is that it cannot be proven to be true by the
adduction of evidence. It would, therefore, be improper to accept that such an
allegation is true. No violence is done to the rule where allegations,
incapable of proof, are not taken as proven.

[
13
]

Respectfully, I think
Operation Dismantle

and the narrow exception to the general principle that pleaded facts are taken
as true at this stage do not apply here. In
Operation Dismantle
, the
Court was referring to situations where the allegations were incapable of being
proven in the sense that the allegation was speculative by nature. The
allegation could not be proven because there could be no evidence to show what
might happen in the future if the U.S. was allowed to test cruise missiles in
Canada. Here the allegations are concrete and refer to actions that the Amnis defendants’
allege have already taken place. In this sense the claims as they are set out
in the counterclaim are capable of being proven and are not speculative.

[
14
]

With regard to the issue of admissibility of
affidavit evidence, I agree with Mr. Holeksa’s statement of the law in
regard to an application pursuant to sub-Rule 9-5(1)(a), but Ms. Pour also
relies also on sub-rules (b), (c) and (d). Mr. Holeksa does not dispute
that under these sub-rules some affidavit evidence may be admitted, however, he
claims that it can be admitted only for very restrictive purposes. Both the plaintiff
and the Amnis defendants rely here on the this Court’s ruling (pursuant to Rule
19(24), the equivalent to Rule 9-5 under the old
Rules
) in
347202 B.C.
Ltd. v. Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce
,
[1995] B.C.J. No. 449
:

18

The
question to be resolved is, for what purpose may evidence be considered?

19

In
Coopers & Lybrand v. Jennings, supra, Huddart J. found that the absence of
a restriction on the adducing of evidence on applications under Rule 19(24)(b),
(c) and (d) made sense because evidence may be “helpful, even necessary, in
determining whether a pleading is ‘unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous, or
vexatious’, or otherwise offends Rule 19 as an abuse of the process of the
court” (p. 5). In respect of Rule 19(24)(a) she reasoned that, “(i)f the only
question on an application is whether the impugned pleading discloses a
reasonable claim, evidence will be superfluous” (p. 5). Similarly, in McGauley
v. Jennings et al.
[1990] B.C.J. No. 2630
(4 December 1990), Vancouver
CA012295, Southin J.A. said: “I am quite unable to see what possible purpose
evidence has on such an application.” (p. 3).

20

If
then, evidence by way of affidavit is helpful in determining whether a pleading
is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous, vexatious or otherwise an abuse of the
process of the Court, it may be considered. I am led, however, to the practical
conclusion that affidavit material which simply asserts facts contrary to those
alleged in the pleadings will rarely be sufficient to establish that an action
is certain to fail. In other words, a court will not strike out a claim as
vexatious or scandalous where affidavit evidence does nothing more than
contradict the allegations contained in the pleadings, although the affidavit
itself will be admitted and considered.

21

To summarize my conclusions, I find that the “plain and obvious”
test applicable to Rule 19(24)(a) applies to subrules (b) and (d). Other
considerations are also applicable to applications under subrules (b) and (d).
The most obvious example of other considerations is that of evidence adduced by
way of affidavit. Such evidence will be considered if it is helpful or
necessary in resolving the questions to be answered but, if the evidence does
nothing more than contradict the allegations in the pleadings, it would rarely
be sufficient to establish that the action is bound to fail.

[
15
]

In deciding whether or not to admit affidavit
evidence the inquiry is twofold. First the court asks for what purpose is the
affidavit evidence being tendered and the second issue to be considered is the
nature of that evidence. Evidence that simply contradicts the facts stated in
the counterclaim will not be helpful. However, evidence that may be helpful in
determining whether a pleading is “unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous,
vexatious or otherwise an abuse of the process of the Court” is admissible and may
be considered.

[
16
]

The dispute here concerns the evidence found in
several affidavits that were filed by Ms. Pour as part of her application
record. There are five affidavits of Amir Behzad Shoolestani, two of Amir
Yashar Shoolestani, and one of Ashraf Razaei Pour.

[
17
]

In his oral and written submissions, Mr. Holeksa
raised a second objection to the admissibility of the affidavit evidence,
especially of Amir Behzad Shoolestani, due to what Mr. Holeksa characterized
as a tendency to misstate facts and legal principles. Mr. Holeksa added
that for this same reason I should not rely on the affidavit material or the
factual statements made in the course of submissions in this application
because he argued that Amir Behzad Shoolestani, who has been acting as agent
for his mother, Ms. Pour, has a history of misleading the Court. However,
I do not think that it is appropriate to decide credibility questions,
particularly credibility questions of that sort, on this application.

[
18
]

I have reviewed the affidavit materials and have
found that for the most part they are not helpful in deciding this application.
Most of the statements in the affidavits, as well as the documents attached to
them, relate to other applications and claims in this ongoing litigation.
Moreover, most of the affidavit evidence relates to the claims of other
plaintiffs and the employment history leading up to the termination of the
other plaintiffs from Amnis.

[
19
]

The only affidavit evidence that relates directly
to this application by Ms. Pour to strike the counterclaim is found in
Amir Behzad Shoolestani’s affidavit #17 dated March 27, 2017 and Ms. Pour’s
affidavit #1 dated October 26, 2016.

[
20
]

In her affidavit Ms. Pour states the
following:

7.         The allegations made by the
Defendants in the Counterclaim against me are all false.

8.         I was not involved in and was not
aware of any communications between Amir Yashar Shoolestani and Innergex or
Kiewit, if any, in 2009 or any other times, as alleged by the Defendants in the
Counterclaim. The Defendants have also not produced any evidence in this
regard.

9.         The Defendants never raised the
allegations made in the Counterclaim to me prior to filing the Counterclaim nor
provided me a complaint letter as alleged in the Counterclaim. The Defendants
have also not produced any evidence in this regard.

10.       Thus,
considering that the Defendants have not plead facts to support a claim against
me and have not produced any evidence in support of their allegations against
me, I am sincerely seeking from Court to dismiss the Counterclaim of the
Defendants with costs.

[
21
]

Essentially, Ms. Pour denies the
allegations in the counterclaim. In this regard, her affidavit evidence does “nothing
more than contradict the allegations contained in the pleadings” (
Canadian
Imperial Bank of Commerce
at para. 20). This type of affidavit
evidence is not admissible on an application under Rule 9-5(1)(a) and is of
limited relevance in considering an application under the other subrules.

[
22
]

In his affidavit dated March 17, 2017, Amir
Behzad Shoolestani attached 22 documents, most of which do not directly
relate to this application. However, several documents attached to the
affidavit are connected to the defamation claim in the Amnis defendants’ counterclaim.
The most important documents in this regard are the two emails dated March 19
and March 29, 2009, which form the basis for the defamation claim. The Amnis defendants
claim that the statements made in these two emails, along with other verbal
statements made on March 19, 2009, were defamatory.

[
23
]

Ms. Pour says that this evidence is
relevant and admissible because the emails arguably could be helpful in
determining whether the pleadings in the counterclaim are unnecessary,
scandalous, frivolous, vexatious or otherwise an abuse of the process of the
Court. Ms. Pour says that the emails support her application by proving
that it was Amir Yashar Shoolestani who sent the emails and not Ms. Pour.
Furthermore, Ms. Pour points to the imprecision in the paraphrasing and
characterization of those statements in the counterclaim as further proof that
the pleadings were both deficient and intended to deter her from proceeding
with her claim.

[
24
]

Regardless of whether or not Ms. Pour’s
conclusions from the emails have validity, I find that this affidavit evidence
relating to those emails is admissible for the limited purpose of determining
whether the pleadings in the counterclaim are scandalous, frivolous or
vexatious.

[
25
]

With that background in mind, I turn to the
arguments advanced by Ms. Pour to strike out the counterclaim.

Is the counterclaim out of time or is it an improper
counterclaim not related to or connected with the subject matter of the main
action?

[
26
]

The parties submit that the
Limitation Act
,
R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 266 (“the
Act
”), is the relevant statute for the
purpose of the claims and counterclaims. Ms. Pour argues that the
defamation claim in the counterclaim is statute barred under
s. 3(2)
of
the
Act
, which states that:

After the
expiration of 2 years after the date on which the right to do so arose a person
may not bring any of the following actions:

…

(c) for
defamation;

[
27
]

The alleged defamatory statements were made on
March 19 and March 29, 2009. The counterclaim was filed March 25, 2015, nearly
six years after the last statement was published.

[
28
]

However, the Amnis defendants submit that an
application under Rule 9-5 is not the appropriate forum to decide a
limitation defence. More importantly, even if it was appropriate to
consider it in the context of this application, the two year limitation period
is not applicable in this case because
s. 4(1)
of the
Act
extends
the limitation period in the case of a counterclaim that is related to or
connected with the subject matter of the original action:

If an action to which this or any other
Act

applies has been commenced, the lapse of time limited for bringing an action is
no bar to

(a) proceedings
by counterclaim, including the adding of a new party as a defendant by
counterclaim,

(b) third
party proceedings,

(c) claims by
way of set off, or

(d) adding or
substituting a new party as plaintiff or defendant,

under any
applicable law, with respect to any claims relating to or connected with the
subject matter of the original action.

[
29
]

In
ASM Capital Corp. v. Mercer International Inc.
et al.
,
1999 BCCA 353
at para.
17
, the Court of Appeal determined
that:

Section 4(1)
of
the
Limitation Act
permits a defendant to bring a counterclaim against a
plaintiff even if the cause of action alleged is statute-barred, provided that
the subject matter of the counterclaim is related to or connected with the
subject matter of the plaintiff’s action.

[See also:
Lui v. West
Granville Manor Ltd.
,
1987 CanLII 164 (BC CA)
,
[1987] 4 WWR 49
; 11 BCLR (2d) 273 (C.A.).]

[
30
]

Thus, the initial question here is whether or
not the counterclaim relates to or is connected with the subject matter of the
original action.

[
31
]

Ms. Pour submits that both the defamation
and the malicious prosecution claims are not related to the subject matter of
her action. She points to the fact that, according to the counterclaim, the
alleged defamatory statements were made and published by Amir Yashar
Shoolestani and Amir Behzad Shoolestani and not her. Furthermore, she points to
the fact that the alleged defamatory statements relate to the engineering
work Amir Behzad Shoolestani and Amir Yashar Shoolestani performed for Amnis
and are not related in any way to her specific claim for monies owed for food
services.

[
32
]

In regard to the malicious prosecution,
Ms. Pour submits that although she was named as a plaintiff in the
original action brought against Ichikawa, Amnis and 10 other corporate
defendants, it was clear that Mr. Ichikawa was, and has always been, truly
the sole defendant in her claim.

[
33
]

Mr. Holeksa, on the other hand, argued that
Ms. Pour was nevertheless a plaintiff in the action against all 12
defendants, which is the basis for the claim of malicious prosecution and abuse
of process. More importantly, in relation to both the defamation and malicious
prosecution claims, Ms. Pour’s action is allegedly a component of a larger
wrongful scheme which lies at the heart of the counterclaim. That is that Ms. Pour
and the other plaintiffs all conspired and coordinated to cause the Amnis defendants
injury by initiating legal action and defaming their names and reputation. Mr. Holeksa’s
argument in this regard is that Ms. Pour’s concurrence in the publishing
of the defamatory statements is sufficient to establish liability for the damages
that flow from that act.

[
34
]

It remains of course to be seen if the Amnis defendants
can prove the factual elements of the alleged conspiracy. Likewise, the Amnis defendants
will bear the onus of convincing the Court that concurrence in the context of
both the defamation and malicious prosecution claims can be enough to establish
liability. I note once again that the facts alleged in the counterclaim are to
be taken to be true for the purposes of this part of the application. In
determining the subject application, I express no opinion on the legal and
factual strength of the Amnis defendants’ counterclaim. At this stage, the only
question I must determine is whether or not the Amnis defendants’ pleaded
theory of the conspiracy as advanced in the counterclaim is related to or
connected with the subject matter of Ms. Pour’s action.

[
35
]

Whether or not a claim is related to or
connected with an existing proceeding is a fact-specific inquiry. Among the
factors to consider are the facts that give rise to the claims, the causes
of action and the possible connection between the relief sought by the parties.
In
ASM Capital Corp.
, the Court of Appeal provided guidance on this
point by stating that:

[27]      On this
question, the learned chambers judge simply said:

[15] I agree
with counsel for the defendant that the proposed amendments are claims that are
“related to or connected with the subject matter of the original action”. I
find there is no limitation bar to the proposed amendments sought.

[28]      With
deference, I disagree. In my view, the amendments are not related to or
connected with the subject matter of the plaintiffs’ action. The plaintiffs’
claim is for breach of contract in respect of the option agreement made between
the parties in the fall of 1990. The amendments seek damages for alleged
breaches of trust against two of the plaintiffs in respect of securities
purchased and sold for a loss by a number of corporations in which the
defendant held a direct or indirect beneficial interest between the fall of
1987 and immediately prior to the date the alleged agreement was made.

[29]      Other
than the identity of the parties, the action and the counterclaim are entirely
separate and distinct from one another; their causes of action are distinct;
their subject matters are distinct; the nature of the alleged damages is
distinct; and the periods of time in which the alleged causes of action arose
are distinct. Accepting the defendant’s allegations as true, the defendant’s
entire cause of action had matured and crystallized prior to the date on which
the plaintiffs allege the agreement was entered into. The defendant denies the
existence and the efficacy of the agreement; it denies its authenticity, the
signature of Mr. Smith; and the authenticity of its corporate seal. The
subject matter of the proposed amendments as well as the subject matter of the
original counterclaim are not related to or predicated on the agreement the
plaintiffs allege.

[30]      To prove
their case, the plaintiffs will not have to lead any evidence in relation to
any of the allegations contained in the counterclaim other than the identity of
the parties. Similarly, the defendant will not have to refer to any matters
alleged in the statement of claim to prove any of the allegations contained in
its counterclaim, amended or otherwise, other than the identity of the parties.
The identity of the parties is not a relevant enquiry for determining whether a
counterclaim is related or connected to the action because
s.4(1)
limits the
relation or connection between the two proceedings to their subject-matter.

[31]      In sum,
the learned chambers judge erred in finding that the subject matter of the
proposed amendments was related to, or connected with, the subject matter of
the original action.

[
36
]

Applying this approach to the facts alleged here
leads me to conclude that the claims brought in the counterclaim are
related to or connected with the subject matter of Ms. Pour’s claim.

[
37
]

According to the Amnis defendants’ theory, Ms. Pour’s
claim, as well as the defamatory statements, are all part of a planned and concerted
effort on the part of the Shoolestani family, including Ms. Pour, to
apply pressure on the Amnis defendants in order to obtain a settlement and
compensation they are not legally entitled to.

[
38
]

Given the Amnis defendants’ theory of the case
and the interrelationship between each of the individual claims of the
plaintiffs against the Amnis defendants, as well as the plaintiffs’ decision to
initially advance their claims together in the same action and against all 12
defendants, I find that the counterclaim is related to or connected with Ms. Pour’s
action.

[
39
]

I wish to emphasize that this finding has no
implication in terms of the likelihood of success or strength of the Amnis defendants’
counterclaim. It of course will be up to the Amnis defendants to prove their
case at trial.

[
40
]

In her submissions Ms. Pour referred to
Lui
v. West Granville Manor Ltd.
,
1987 CanLII 164 (BC CA)
, [1987] 4 WWR 49, 11 BCLR (2d) 273 (C.A.). As
I understood the argument of Ms. Pour’s agent, it was that the “relation
back” theory is applicable here and Mr. Shoolestani suggested it has the
effect of overriding
s. 4(1)
of the
Limitation Act
. If the
counterclaim was taken to have been made at, or relates back to, the time
of the original action, it would, he argues, be out of time.

[
41
]

I cannot accept this argument. The main reason I
must reject this argument is that the Court of Appeal itself in
Lui

rejected the “relation back” theory for circumstances such as these and said as
follows:

So, based on the
wording of s-s 4(1), the terms of the report of the Law Reform
Commissioners, and the cases on what started out as s. 80A of the
Motor
Vehicle Act,
I have concluded that the legislative purpose underlying s‑s 4(1)
was to eliminate any limitation defence in all proceedings described in paras. (a)
to (d) of that sub-section. Sub-section 4(1) must be considered to bear the
meaning that carries that purpose into effect.

That conclusion
provides the answer to the first question I have posed. It also raises the
subsidiary issue of how to reconcile s-s 4(1) with s. 9.

In the Daco case, Mr. Justice
Aikins, for the Court, adopted the “relation back” theory. The effect of that
theory is to treat the subordinate proceedings, for limitation purposes,
as
having
been begun on the date that the main action was begun. That theory does indeed
reconcile s-s 4(1) with s. 9. But, in the Daco case, the question of
whether s-s 4(1) completely eliminates all limitation periods was not fully
argued. In this case, after full argument,
I have concluded that the effect
of s-s 4(1) is to eliminate any limitation defence from the subordinate
proceedings. If the defence is eliminated, the cause of action cannot be
regarded as having been extinguished, and the “relation back” theory is wholly
irrelevant.
What need is there to have any deemed starting date for the
subordinate proceedings, for limitation purposes, if, no matter when the
subordinate proceedings were to be treated as having been started, no
limitation defence is to be available?

There is another
reason why the “relation back” theory is not appropriate to effect the
reconciliation between s-s 4(1) and s. 9. It is that the “relation
back” theory does not operate correctly in those cases where the running of the
limitation period in the main action is postponed throughout a period of
minority, or other disability, under s. 7. It may be that when the main
action is eventually brought, perhaps long after the normal limitation period
has expired, there are essential subordinate proceedings, perhaps a third party
claim for contribution or indemnity, that could never have been brought
earlier, but which it would be unjust to prevent. Sub-section 4(1) is intended
to permit those subordinate proceedings without the raising of a limitation
defence. But the “relation back” theory would retain the limitation defence and
for that reason would contradict s-s 4(1).

So, in my opinion, it would be inappropriate to
adopt the “relation back” theory. Instead, the appropriate principle to apply
is that, in cases of legislative inconsistency, the more specific provision
should prevail over the more general provision. So, even where s. 9 had
gone into effect to extinguish the cause of action that was to be the subject
matter of the subordinate proceedings, once those proceedings were begun,
without being struck out, the more specific provisions of s-s 4(1) would
apply, the lapse of time would cease to be a bar, the extinguishment would
cease, and the cause of action would revive.

(at pages 11-2)

[Emphasis added.]

[
42
]

For the purposes of this application, I find
that the counterclaim against Ms. Pour is sufficiently related to or
connected with Ms. Pour’s claim. Accordingly s. 4(1) of the
Limitation
Act
applies and the limitation period is not applicable to the counterclaim
against Ms. Pour for defamation.

[
43
]

Accordingly the first two arguments advanced by Ms. Pour
to strike out the counterclaim must fail.

Do the pleadings show a cause of action?

[
44
]

Ms. Pour relies on sub-Rule 9-5(1)(a) which
stipulates that a pleading that discloses no reasonable claim may be struck.
She claims that in respect to both the defamation and malicious
prosecution claims, the counterclaim does not disclose a cause of action
because the alleged wrongful acts are attributed to the other plaintiffs and
the material facts stated in the counterclaim do not relate to Ms. Pour.

[
45
]

In regard to the defamation claim, Ms. Pour
points once more to the fact that the emails were drafted and sent by others.
With regard to the claim of malicious prosecution, Ms. Pour argues that it
was always known to the Amnis defendants that her claim was only against Mr. Ichikawa
even if she appeared as a plaintiff in the initial action which named Mr. Ichikawa,
Amnis and 10 other corporate defendants. In support of this submission
Ms. Pour refers to her Amended Notice of Civil Claim where she states that
her claim is only against Mr. Ichikawa. She also refers to my previous decision
(indexed as
2017 BCSC 139
) to allow her to amend her Notice of Civil Claim, in
which I noted that:

[7]        In her initial pleading Ms. Pour
advanced a claim in contract for monies owing for food services that she
said she provided. Although the plea was somewhat imprecise because there was
no reference to it in the prayer for relief, it is clear that this claim was
advanced by her in contract.

[8]
The
Amnis defendants acknowledge this. According to their counsel’s written
submission: “Although the Amended Notice of Civil Claim is not as precise as it
should be, the Amnis defendants previously understood the claim was advanced
solely against Ichikawa and solely in contract.”
The Amnis defendants go on
to say: “… the true amendments are to advance claims for
quantum meruit

and unjust enrichment.”

[Emphasis added.]

[
46
]

Ms. Pour submits that, given that the claim
for malicious prosecution is based on the plaintiffs’ attempt to apply pressure
on Mr. Ichikawa and Amnis by naming their corporate clients in the initial
action, the Amnis defendants’ admission that they have always understood
her claim to be only against Mr. Ichikawa effectively acknowledges that
she had nothing to do with the action taken against the other defendants.

[
47
]

The Amnis defendants’ submit that in both the
Notice of Civil Claim and the Amended Notice of Civil Claim Ms. Pour
articulated her claim as “The Plaintiffs claim against the Defendants”.
Furthermore, in the Amnis defendants’ initial Response to Civil Claim dated
March 25, 2015, they claimed that “Pour was never hired by, employed by or had
any contractual relationship with Amnis Engineering Ltd. or with any other
Defendant in this action”. According to Mr. Holeksa, this demonstrates
that the Amnis defendants contemplated that, like the other plaintiffs, Ms. Pour’s
claim was initially against all 12 defendants.

[
48
]

In any event, Mr. Holeksa urged the Court
to consider Ms. Pour’s claim within the broader context of the dispute
between the Shoolestani family and the Amnis defendants. He claims that when
considered in this context, Ms. Pour’s claim is one component of what
the Amnis defendants allege is a larger scheme of the Shoolestani family to
unlawfully force the Amnis defendants to settle.

[
49
]

In
Watson v. Bank of America Corporation
,

2014 BCSC 532
, the Court summarized the test for striking out a claim for not
disclosing a cause of action:

[60]      Subsection
(a) requires that the pleadings disclose a cause of action. This requirement is
assessed on the same standard as on a motion to strike pleadings under Rule
9-5(1)(a). Accordingly, the plaintiff satisfies this requirement unless it is
plain and obvious that the claim cannot succeed:
Hollick
at para. 25;

Microsoft
at para. 63. For this analysis, the Court must assume
that all the pleaded facts are true unless they are patently unreasonable or
incapable of proof. Further, a claim must not be struck merely because it is
novel or complex:
Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc
.,
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R.
959 at 980.

[
50
]

A similar approach was applied in an earlier case
under the old
Rules
:

[34]      To succeed on an application under
Rule 19(24)(a) it must be established that it is “plain and obvious” that the
pleading discloses no reasonable cause of action:
Hunt v. Carey Canada
,
1990
CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959 (S.C.C.). If there is any doubt it should
be resolved in favour of permitting the pleadings to stand:
McGauley v.
British Columbia
(1989),
1989 CanLII 2809 (BC CA)
, 39 B.C.L.R. (2d) 223
(B.C.C.A.). The court should proceed on the assumption that all the facts pled
are true:
Helman v. Brown
(1966),
1966 CanLII 597 (BC CA)
, 57 W.W.R. 608 (B.C.C.A.). The only
question then is whether the facts disclose a cause of action:
Minnes v.
Minnes
(1962),
1962 CanLII 350 (BC CA)
, 39 W.W.R. 112 (B.C.C.A.);
McNaughton
v. Baker
(1988),
1988 CanLII 3036 (BC CA)
, 25 B.C.L.R. (2d) 17 (C.A.). In
other words, as long as the pleadings disclose a triable issue, either as it
exists, or as it may be amended, then the issue should go to trial. The mere
fact that the case is weak or not likely to succeed is no ground for striking
it out under the provisions of Rule 19(24):
Minnes, supra
.

(
Citizens for
Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress
,
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, [1999] CarswellBC
2111; [1999] BCJ No 2160 (QL) (S.C.)

[
51
]

Applying this test to the subject case, I cannot
find that it is “plain and obvious” that the Amnis defendants’ pleadings
disclose no reasonable cause of action or a triable issue. As stated in
Watson
,
a claim ought not to be struck merely because it is complex or novel. The Amnis
defendants advance a factual and legal theory in their counterclaim that Ms. Pour
was involved in a conspiracy aimed at applying pressure on the Amnis defendants
through a concerted effort in collaboration with the other plaintiffs. This
alleged scheme consisted of publishing defamatory statements about Mr. Ichikawa
and Amnis and initiating improper legal action against all defendants including
the clients of Amnis. The counterclaim states this to be the factual and legal
basis of the Amnis defendants’ claim. In relation to the defamation claim, the
counterclaim reads as follows:

14.       Although the emails were sent by
Amir Yashr Shoolestani, the emails were sent with the agreement and concurrence
of the other Defendants by Counterclaim and the other Defendants by
Counterclaim are equally responsible and liable for the emails.

15.       Although
the works were spoken by Amir Yashr Shoolestani and Amir Behzad Shoolestani,
the words were spoken with the agreement and concurrence of the other
Defendants by Counterclaim and the other Defendants by Counterclaim are equally
responsible and liable for the words spoken.

In relation to
the malicious prosecution claim the counterclaim states:

26.       The
Plaintiffs, and each of them, have conspired to injure Glen Ichikawa, Amnis Engineering
Ltd., and Kawa Engineering Ltd. by bringing this Notice of Civil Claim.

In this last paragraph the Amnis defendants
are referring to the original Notice of Civil Claim in which Ms. Pour’s
claim was raised along with the claims of the other plaintiffs and was one
component of the alleged malicious prosecution and abuse of process.

[
52
]

While the Amnis defendants may be raising a
complex claim which possibly includes an element of legal novelty, that is not
a sufficient reason to order that the pleadings be struck. Assuming the truth
of the material facts that are pleaded, i.e. that Ms. Pour participated in
the conspiracy and was actively involved in both the publication of the alleged
defamatory statements and the initiating of the claim against all the
defendants, including clients of Amnis, for an improper purpose, the counterclaim
reveals a triable issue. Ms. Pour’s argument under this head
must fail.

Is the claim properly pleaded in the counterclaim?

[
53
]

The fourth argument raised by Ms. Pour to
strike the counterclaim relates to discrepancies between the alleged
defamatory emails and their characterization and paraphrasing in the counterclaim.
Ms. Pour argues that the Amnis defendants ought to have cited the emails
precisely and that this failure further shows that the counterclaim is “scandalous,
frivolous or vexatious”. According to Ms. Pour, the Amnis defendants’
failure to accurately quote the emails also constitutes a fundamental deficiency
in the pleadings and the Amnis defendants should not now be permitted to
amend the claim.

[
54
]

Mr. Holeksa conceded that in the
counterclaim the emails were not accurately quoted but argues that in an
attempt to be concise he chose to simply paraphrase the contents of those
emails. More importantly, Mr. Holeksa submits that the paraphrasing of the
emails in the counterclaim is a fair reading of their contents and the ideas
they were meant to express.

[
55
]

While I agree that the Amnis defendants should
have accurately quoted the emails, I do not think that their failure to do
so is fatal to the counterclaim. Striking a pleading is a draconian remedy that
should not be granted where the deficiency can be cured through an amendment or
other less severe orders (see
Sahyoun v. Ho
,
2015 BCSC 392
at para.
144
,
appeal dismissed
2017 BCCA 96
; see also
Royal Bank of Canada v. Roberts
,

2014 BCSC 1797
). I find that the failure of the Amnis defendants can be cured through
a more proportionate remedy which is to allow the Amnis defendants to amend
their counterclaim and properly quote the emails. I grant the Amnis defendants
leave to amend their pleadings in that respect.

Does the subsequent discontinuance by Ms. Pour of the
original claim constitute termination of the proceedings for the tort of
malicious prosecution?

[
56
]

The fifth argument Ms. Pour raised in both
her oral and written submissions relates to the malicious prosecution claim.
Ms. Pour argues that a claim for malicious prosecution can only be made
once the initial proceeding which is the subject of the claim for malicious
prosecution has terminated. Since Ms. Pour’s claim for monies owing to her
is still being advanced, she argues that the Amnis defendants cannot raise a
claim for malicious prosecution at this time.

[
57
]

Although the tort of abuse of process which is
asserted in this case does not require that the proceeding commenced for an
improper purpose be terminated (
311165 B.C. Ltd v Canada (A.G.),

2017
BCCA 196
), the tort of malicious prosecution requires that the proceedings be
terminated in favour of the claimant for there to be a cause of action. In
support of her submission, Ms. Pour relies on
Nelles v. Ontario
,

1989 CanLII 77 (SCC)
, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 170 at para.
42
, where the Supreme Court of Canada set out
the four necessary elements for a successful malicious prosecution claim:

There are four necessary elements which must be
proved for a plaintiff to succeed in an action for malicious prosecution:

a) the proceedings must have been initiated by
the defendant;

b) the proceedings must have terminated in
favour of the plaintiff;

c) the absence of reasonable and probable
cause;

d) malice, or a primary purpose other than that
of carrying the law into effect.

(See J. G. Fleming,
The Law of Torts (5th ed. 1977), at p. 598.)

[
58
]

Ms. Pour points to the fact that her claim was
ongoing when the counterclaim was initiated, and is still ongoing, and therefore
element (b) is not met.

[
59
]

Mr. Holeksa suggests that the fact that Ms. Pour
discontinued her initial claim against some of the defendants originally named
in the action constitutes “termination” of that proceeding for the purposes of
the malicious prosecution cause of action.

[
60
]

Clearly when the counterclaim was initiated the Amnis
defendants did not have a cause of action for malicious prosecution.

[
61
]

I understood Mr. Holeksa’s position to be
that if there was no cause of action when the counterclaim was filed, that was
rectified when Ms. Pour filed a notice of discontinuance on May 3, 2016 in
which she discontinued her action against all of the defendants except Mr. Ichikawa.
I disagree.

[
62
]

If the discontinuance by Ms. Pour was to
make it clear that her claim, that she is still pursuing, is against Mr. Ichikawa
rather than his related corporate entities, I do not think that discontinuance is
a “termination” of the proceeding “in favour of the plaintiff” for the purposes
of this tort.

[
63
]

I have concluded that there was no cause of
action for malicious prosecution when the counterclaim was initiated and that
defect has not been cured.

Conclusion

[
64
]

Accordingly, Ms. Pour’s application is
dismissed with the exception that paragraph 4 of the prayer for relief seeking “Damages
for Malicious Prosecution” is struck from the counterclaim against her.

[
65
]

Costs of this application will be in the cause.

“The Honourable Mr. Justice Sigurdson”
